messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 61
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Sculptor
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 41

She is 61, a South Eastern Asian woman who has spent most of her adult life shaping clay, stone, and metal into human forms. She talks about sculpture as if it is a way of listening. In her studio, she says, she has always known how to wait, how to let tension reveal itself slowly under her hands. What she cannot do now is bear sudden sound. The strike of a dropped tool, the scrape of metal, even her husband calling to her from another room can make her whole body jump before she knows why.

The event she returns to happened four years ago, on an ordinary afternoon at a crowded market. She had gone there looking for old brass utensils and discarded wood, things she often collects for mixed-media work. She remembers the heat, the smell of frying garlic and fish sauce, the close movement of people negotiating prices. Ahead of her, a motorbike clipped a pedestrian at the edge of the road. At first she thought it was a near miss, the kind of urban chaos people brush off and keep walking through. Then she saw the woman fall backward and strike her head on the curb.

She says time changed texture in that moment. The crowd gathered and broke apart at once. Someone shouted for help. The motorbike slid on its side. She stood only a few feet away and saw the injured woman’s eyes open but unfocused, her mouth moving without sound, blood beginning to spread beneath her hair. She remembers the woman’s young son, maybe eight or nine, tugging at her sleeve and crying for his mother to get up. That part stays with her most fiercely: not only the blood and helplessness, but the child’s voice, raw and disbelieving. She froze. She did not kneel beside them, did not call out instructions, did not do any of the things she later told herself a decent person should have done. Others moved in. Someone called emergency services. She stood holding a bag of metal scraps until her fingers hurt from gripping it. Even after she got home, she could still hear the child crying in the market noise.

In the weeks after, she tells herself she is just shaken. She avoids that part of town and says it is because parking there is difficult. But the woman’s face appears when she is washing rice, when she closes her eyes in the shower, when she lies down beside her husband. At night she wakes with her heart pounding, sometimes after dreams in which her own daughter, now grown, is lying on the pavement while strangers watch. In the dreams she tries to move but cannot. She becomes afraid of sleep because of how violently she returns from it.

Her husband notices first that she is no longer herself in the studio. She used to work for hours with music playing, absorbed and steady. Now she keeps the radio off because layered sounds unsettle her. She positions herself so she can see the door. If a delivery truck backfires outside, she startles so hard she has once cut her palm on a wire armature. She begins leaving projects unfinished, especially figures with faces. When she tries to sculpt expressions of tenderness or calm, the features shift under her hands into something slack, injured, or frightened. She grows irritated with herself and then ashamed. She tells clients she is slowing down with age, but privately she wonders whether something in her has become damaged and fixed.

Her world narrows in quiet ways. She declines invitations to busy festivals she once loved. She no longer goes with her husband to open-air markets, and if grandchildren run ahead near a street, she becomes tense and sharp, calling them back too quickly. She scans intersections automatically. In crowds she watches for falls, collisions, signs that someone is about to be hurt. She says she feels foolish because she knows, rationally, that not every street corner holds disaster, yet her body behaves as if catastrophe is waiting just outside her field of vision.

What troubles her nearly as much as fear is the guilt. She speaks about the injured woman as if she failed her personally. She replays the scene with revisions: in one version she kneels and comforts the boy; in another she presses cloth to the wound; in another she speaks clearly and takes charge. Instead, she remembers standing still. “Like stone,” she says, with a bitterness that catches her because stone is the material she has trusted all her life. Since then, she is less certain of her own character. She wonders what kind of person freezes while a child screams.

Now, years later, the market accident continues to organize her days more than she wants to admit. She remains loving with her family and disciplined in her work, but she moves through life with a layer of vigilance that never fully lifts. She tries to return to the studio each morning, unlocking the door, laying out her tools, placing her palms on the cool surface of unfinished pieces. Some days the work steadies her. Some days a small sound pulls her instantly back to the curb, the blood, the child’s voice, and the terrible feeling of being present for another person’s suffering while unable to stop it.
